191: The mean is the arithmetic average of all values; the median is the middle value when the data is sorted. The mean uses every value, so outliers pull it strongly, while the median depends only on rank order, which makes it robust. Use the mean for roughly symmetric data without extreme outliers, and the median for skewed data such as income, house prices, or response times.
192: The median is better when the distribution is skewed or contains outliers, when the data is ordinal, or when a few extreme values would distort the mean. For example, median household income represents a typical household better than mean income because billionaires inflate the mean.
193: Variance measures the average squared deviation from the mean: it quantifies how spread out the data is. Because deviations are squared, variance is in squared units and is sensitive to outliers. Standard deviation, its square root, brings the measure back to the original units.
194: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and expresses spread in the same units as the data. Roughly 68% of a normal distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean and 95% within two. It is the most commonly reported measure of dispersion.
195: Covariance measures whether two variables move together: positive means they increase together, negative means one rises while the other falls. Its magnitude depends on the variables' units, so it is hard to compare across pairs of variables. Correlation is the normalized form of covariance.
196: Correlation standardizes covariance to the range -1 to +1, making strength and direction of a linear relationship comparable across datasets. A value near 1 means a strong positive linear relation, near -1 a strong negative one, and near 0 little linear relation. Correlation still does not imply causation.
197: Pearson correlation measures linear relationships between continuous variables and is sensitive to outliers. Spearman correlation ranks the data first and measures monotonic relationships, so it captures any consistently increasing or decreasing trend and is robust to outliers. Use Spearman for skewed data, ordinal data, or non-linear monotonic patterns.
198: Correlation means two variables move together; causation means a change in one produces a change in the other. A third hidden variable (confounder), reverse causality, or pure coincidence can create correlation without any causal link, like ice-cream sales correlating with drowning deaths because both rise in summer. Establishing causation requires controlled experiments, A/B tests, or causal-inference methods.
199: Skewness measures the asymmetry of a distribution. Positive (right) skew has a long right tail, so the mean exceeds the median, as with income; negative (left) skew has a long left tail and the mean is below the median. Many models assume roughly symmetric inputs, so skewness often motivates transformations such as log.
200: Kurtosis measures how heavy the tails of a distribution are compared with a normal distribution. High kurtosis means more extreme outliers occur more often; low kurtosis means thin tails and few extremes. It matters in risk analysis where rare extreme events dominate outcomes.
201: An outlier is a data point far from the rest of the distribution. It can be an error (sensor glitch, typo) or a genuine rare value (a fraudulent transaction). Detect them with IQR fences, z-scores, or isolation forests, and decide to remove, cap, or keep them based on the business meaning, because fraud detection treats outliers as the signal itself.
202: The IQR is the range between the 25th percentile (Q1) and the 75th percentile (Q3), covering the middle 50% of the data. Points below Q1 - 1.5*IQR or above Q3 + 1.5*IQR are commonly flagged as outliers. It is robust because it ignores the extreme tails.
203: A z-score expresses how many standard deviations a value is from the mean: z = (x - mean) / sd. Values with |z| greater than about 3 are often treated as outliers for roughly normal data. Z-scores also allow comparison of values across differently scaled variables.
204: A population is the entire group you want conclusions about; a sample is the subset you actually observe. We compute statistics (sample mean) to estimate parameters (population mean). Poor sampling produces biased estimates no matter how sophisticated the model is.
205: Population variance divides the squared deviations by N, while sample variance divides by n-1. The n-1 Bessel correction compensates for underestimating spread when the sample mean is used instead of the true population mean. Without it, sample variance would be systematically too small.
206: The standard error is the standard deviation of a sampling statistic, most often the sample mean: sd divided by the square root of n. It describes how much the statistic would vary across repeated samples. It shrinks as sample size grows, which is why bigger samples give more precise estimates.
207: A confidence interval is a range computed from sample data that would contain the true parameter in roughly 95% of repeated samples (for a 95% CI). It combines an estimate with its uncertainty: estimate plus or minus about two standard errors. Wider intervals signal less certainty.
208: It does not mean there is a 95% probability that the true value lies inside this particular interval. The parameter is fixed; the randomness is in the sampling procedure. A 95% CI means: if we repeated the sampling and interval construction many times, about 95% of those intervals would capture the true value.
209: The Central Limit Theorem says the distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows, regardless of the population's shape, with standard error sd/sqrt(n). It usually holds well around n >= 30. It is the foundation for confidence intervals, z-tests, and t-tests.
210: The Law of Large Numbers states that the sample average converges to the true expected value as the number of observations grows. It explains why long-run averages stabilize, like a casino's edge emerging over many bets. It says nothing about short-run correction, which is the gambler's fallacy.
211: Sampling bias occurs when the sampling procedure systematically favors some parts of the population, so the sample is not representative. Example: surveying only users of one app platform undercounts the other platform's experience. The fix is proper random or stratified sampling.
212: Selection bias is any systematic distortion caused by how subjects are selected or self-select into the sample. A classic case is survivorship bias: analyzing only companies that survived the decade. It distorts conclusions even with a huge sample size.
213: Survivorship bias is a selection bias where only surviving entities remain visible in the data. Studying only successful startups overestimates average success rates because failed ones dropped out of view. Always ask which entities are missing from the dataset and why.
214: Simpson's paradox is a trend that appears in aggregated data but reverses within every subgroup. It happens when group sizes are imbalanced and a lurking variable drives both group membership and the outcome. Always segment before concluding, especially across cohorts with different sizes.
215: The gambler's fallacy is the mistaken belief that independent events are 'due' to balance out, like expecting heads after five tails in a row. Each fair coin toss remains independent with 50% probability. In ML terms: past draws do not shift probabilities in i.i.d. data.
216: The base-rate fallacy is ignoring the prior frequency of an event when judging how likely it is, which is why a test with 99% accuracy can still mean most positives are false positives for a rare disease. Bayes' theorem corrects for this by multiplying the likelihood by the base rate. It is central to fraud and anomaly detection.
217: Probability quantifies uncertainty of an event on a 0 to 1 scale, where 0 is impossible and 1 is certain. Basic rules include the addition rule for unions, the multiplication rule for independent events, and that probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes sum to 1. It is the language every statistical model is built on.
218: Conditional probability P(A|B) is the probability of A given that B has occurred: P(A and B) divided by P(B). It updates beliefs with evidence, and it is the core of Bayes' theorem. For independent events, P(A|B) equals P(A).
219: Independent events do not influence each other's probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). Dependent events do: knowing one changes the probability of the other, like drawing cards without replacement. Most ML models either assume feature independence (Naive Bayes) or explicitly model dependence.
220: Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen: P(A and B) = 0, so P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Example: a single customer cannot churn and stay in the same period. This is why you subtract the overlap in the general addition rule only when events are not exclusive.
221: Bayes' theorem updates a probability with evidence: posterior equals likelihood times prior divided by evidence, P(H|D) = P(D|H)P(H)/P(D). It converts 'probability of data given hypothesis' into 'probability of hypothesis given data'. Spam filters, medical diagnosis, and Naive Bayes all run on it.
222: A disease affects 1% of people (prior). A test detects it with 99% sensitivity and has 5% false positives. P(disease | positive) = (0.99 x 0.01) / (0.99 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99) which is about 0.167, so only roughly a one-in-six chance despite the accurate test, because the disease is rare.
223: The prior P(H) is your belief before seeing data; the likelihood P(D|H) is how probable the observed data is if the hypothesis holds; the posterior P(H|D) is the updated belief after combining them with Bayes' theorem. As data accumulates, the posterior of one step becomes the prior of the next.
224: Expected value is the probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes: sum of p_i times x_i. It is what you get on average per trial in the long run. Decision-making under uncertainty compares options by expected value or expected utility, not by best case.
225: The variance of a random variable is E[(X - E[X])^2], the expected squared deviation from its mean. It quantifies dispersion of the random variable itself. Standard deviation, its square root, is easier to interpret because it shares the variable's units.
226: Conditional expectation E[X|Y=y] is the average of X when Y is known to equal y; as a function of y it is called the regression function. It is the best possible predictor of X given Y under squared-error loss. Regression models are direct estimates of conditional expectations.
227: A Bernoulli distribution models a single trial with two outcomes: success with probability p, failure with 1-p. Mean is p, variance is p(1-p). It is the building block of the binomial distribution and appears in any yes/no modeling such as churn.
228: The binomial distribution counts successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with success probability p: P(k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k). Mean is np, variance is np(1-p). Use it for counts of successes in a fixed number of tries, like conversions out of 100 clicks.
229: The Poisson distribution models counts of events in a fixed interval of time or space when events happen independently at a constant average rate lambda: P(k) = lambda^k e^(-lambda) / k!. Mean and variance are both lambda. Typical uses are server errors per hour or support tickets per day.
230: The normal distribution is the bell-shaped distribution defined by its mean mu and standard deviation sigma, symmetric around the mean. About 68/95/99.7% of mass lies within one, two, and three standard deviations. It arises naturally via the CLT and underlies linear regression's error assumptions.
231: The uniform distribution gives equal probability to all values in an interval [a, b]. Mean is (a+b)/2, variance is (b-a)^2/12. It is used for random initialization of weights, simulating unknown bounded quantities, and as a prior with no preference.
232: The exponential distribution models waiting time between independent events in a Poisson process with rate lambda: density lambda e^(-lambda x). It is memoryless, meaning past waiting does not change future probability. Used for time between user actions, failures, or arrivals.
233: The Gamma distribution generalizes the exponential to waiting time for the k-th event, or sums of k exponentials. It is defined by shape k and rate lambda, is flexible and right-skewed, and is used for queueing times and as a conjugate prior for Poisson rates.
234: The Beta distribution lives on [0,1] and is defined by two shape parameters alpha and beta, making it ideal for modeling probabilities and proportions. It is the conjugate prior for the binomial: Beta(1+a, 1+b) after observing a successes and b failures. A/B testing and Thompson sampling rely on it.
235: The chi-square distribution arises from the sum of squared standard normals with k degrees of freedom. It is right-skewed and underlies the chi-square goodness-of-fit and independence tests, which compare observed versus expected counts.
236: The t-distribution looks like a normal distribution but with heavier tails, defined by degrees of freedom. It accounts for extra uncertainty when the sample standard deviation replaces an unknown population sd. As n grows it converges to the normal, which is why the t-test works for small samples.
237: The F-distribution is the ratio of two scaled chi-square variables and appears in ANOVA and F-tests for comparing variances or overall model significance. It is right-skewed and indexed by two degrees-of-freedom parameters, one per group.
238: Match the distribution to the data-generating process: Bernoulli or binomial for counts of successes, Poisson for event counts per interval, exponential for waiting times, normal for averaged continuous measurements, beta for proportions, t for small-sample means, chi-square and F for testing. Identify the mechanism first, then the distribution follows.
239: The PMF gives probabilities of discrete outcomes and sums to 1; the PDF gives density for continuous variables, so you integrate it to get probabilities and the probability of any exact point is zero. The CDF gives the cumulative probability up to a value for both types, and P(a < X <= b) equals F(b) - F(a).
240: The normal distribution appears everywhere because of the Central Limit Theorem: sums and averages of many small independent effects tend toward normality, whatever each effect's own distribution. Measurement errors, biological traits, and sample means all behave this way. It is also mathematically convenient, being fully described by two parameters.
241: The null hypothesis H0 is the default claim of no effect or no difference, such as 'the new button does not change conversion'. Hypothesis tests assume H0 and ask how surprising the observed data would be under it. We reject or fail to reject it; we never prove it true.
242: The alternative hypothesis H1 is what you typically want to demonstrate: an effect or difference exists. It can be two-sided (different) or one-sided (greater or less). The test's power and critical region depend on how H1 is framed.
243: A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting a true null hypothesis, like shipping a change that actually does nothing. Its probability is controlled by the significance level alpha, typically 5%. Stricter alpha reduces false positives but raises false negatives.
244: A Type II error is a false negative: failing to reject a null that is actually false, like missing a genuinely better model. Its probability is beta, and power is 1 - beta. Larger effects, bigger samples, and less noise all reduce Type II errors.
245: Statistical power is the probability of detecting a real effect, equal to 1 - beta. It depends on effect size, sample size, alpha, and noise. Underpowered A/B tests are a leading cause of 'flat' results that were really undetected wins, so power analysis before the experiment is best practice.
246: The significance level alpha is the threshold for false positives you accept in advance, usually 0.05. A p-value below alpha leads to rejecting the null hypothesis. Alpha should reflect the real cost of a false positive, which is why medical and fraud contexts may demand much stricter levels.
247: The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as what you got, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, nor the probability of chance. Small p-values mean the data would be surprising under H0.
248: p < 0.05 means: if the null were true, data this extreme would occur under 5% of the time. It says nothing about the probability that the hypothesis itself is true; that requires a Bayesian posterior and a prior. Confusing the two is the classic p-value misreading, and base rates matter enormously for rare hypotheses.
249: A one-tailed test checks for an effect in a specified direction and puts all alpha in one tail, giving more power for that direction. A two-tailed test checks for any difference and splits alpha across both tails. Choose two-tailed unless the opposite direction is truly meaningless or irrelevant.
250: The z-test evaluates hypotheses about means or proportions when the population standard deviation is known or the sample is large, using the normal distribution via the CLT. Example: checking whether click-through rate differs from a known baseline with millions of observations.
251: The t-test compares means when the population standard deviation is unknown and estimated from the sample, especially with small n. It uses the t-distribution's heavier tails to account for that extra uncertainty. Variants include one-sample, two-sample, and paired t-tests.
252: A paired t-test compares two measurements on the same subjects, like before versus after, by analyzing the differences, which removes between-subject noise. An independent t-test compares the means of two separate groups. Pairing when possible is more powerful because each subject acts as their own control.
253: The chi-square test compares observed and expected counts: goodness-of-fit checks whether categorical data matches a distribution, and the test of independence checks whether two categorical variables are associated, like device type versus churn. It needs expected counts of at least about 5 per cell.
254: ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) tests whether the means of three or more groups differ by comparing between-group variance to within-group variance, producing an F statistic. A significant F says at least one group differs; post-hoc tests then identify which. It controls the Type I error rate better than running many t-tests.
255: The Mann-Whitney U test is a non-parametric alternative to the independent t-test that compares whether one distribution tends to produce larger values than the other, using ranks. Use it when data is ordinal, skewed, or violates normality assumptions.
256: The Wilcoxon test is the rank-based alternative to the paired t-test: the signed-rank version compares paired differences, and the rank-sum version (equivalent to Mann-Whitney) compares independent samples. It works on differences' ranks rather than their raw values, so outliers matter less.
257: The t-test assumes roughly independent observations, approximately normal data or residuals (or a large enough sample for the CLT), and similar variances across groups for the standard two-sample form. Heavy skew, extreme outliers, or strong dependence can break it, which is when rank-based tests are safer.
258: When assumptions are violated, p-values and error rates become unreliable: false-positive rates inflate or power collapses. Remedies include transformations (log for skew), robust or non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney, bootstrap), variance corrections (Welch), or better experiment design. Check assumptions before trusting results.
259: Testing many hypotheses at once makes false positives almost inevitable: with 20 independent tests at alpha 0.05, you expect about one false discovery. Remedies are Bonferroni-style corrections, FDR control, or hierarchical testing. This is why dashboards full of metrics need correction, not just one-off A/B tests.
260: The Bonferroni correction divides alpha by the number of tests, so with 10 tests you require p < 0.005 for each. It strongly controls the chance of any false positive (FWER) but is conservative, reducing power. It is best when false positives are very costly or the test count is modest.
261: The false discovery rate (FDR) controls the expected proportion of false positives among the discoveries you declare, rather than the chance of even one. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure enforces it and retains far more power than Bonferroni. It is the standard for screening many features or metrics.
262: Statistical significance says an effect is unlikely under the null; practical significance says the effect is big enough to matter. With huge samples, trivial differences become significant. Always report effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside p-values and judge business impact.
285: Machine learning is the practice of fitting models to data so they make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed with rules. Types include supervised learning from labeled examples, unsupervised learning of structure, and reinforcement learning from reward. It powers ranking, forecasting, fraud detection, and recommendation systems.
286: Supervised learning trains on input-output pairs, like features to churn label, and predicts outputs for new inputs. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data through clustering, dimensionality reduction, or density estimation. The choice depends on whether you have labels and what the business question needs.
287: Semi-supervised learning uses a small labeled set plus a large unlabeled set, exploiting structure such as clusters or consistency to improve over labels alone. It shines when labels are expensive, like medical imaging, but unlabeled data is plentiful. Techniques include self-training and label propagation.
288: Self-supervised learning generates its own labels from raw data, like predicting the next word or a masked patch, then fine-tunes on the downstream task. It is how LLMs and modern vision models learn from internet-scale data without manual labels. Pretraining plus fine-tuning is the dominant paradigm.
289: Batch (offline) learning trains on the full dataset at once and is redeployed periodically; it is simpler and reproducible. Online learning updates the model incrementally as new data streams in, adapting to drift but vulnerable to bad data and harder to audit. Choose based on data velocity and drift speed.
290: Parametric models fix the number of parameters in advance, like linear regression's coefficients, and are fast with strong assumptions. Non-parametric models grow with the data, like kNN and decision trees, and are flexible but data-hungry and can overfit. The trade-off is bias versus flexibility.
291: Generative models learn the joint distribution P(X, Y) or P(X) and can generate new samples, like Naive Bayes or diffusion models. Discriminative models learn P(Y|X) directly, like logistic regression, and are usually better at pure prediction with the same data. Generative models add synthesis and richer uncertainty modeling.
292: Bias is error from overly simple assumptions, causing underfitting; variance is error from sensitivity to the particular training sample, causing overfitting. Increasing model complexity lowers bias and raises variance. The total error combines both plus irreducible noise.
293: The bias-variance tradeoff is choosing model complexity to balance systematic error against sensitivity to training data. Tools include regularization, more data, ensembles, and validation curves. The goal is minimizing total error on unseen data, not minimizing training error.
294: Underfitting is when the model is too simple to capture the signal, showing high error on both training and validation data. Fixes include a more expressive model, better features, less regularization, and longer training. Diagnose it when training error itself is high.
295: Overfitting is when the model memorizes noise in the training set, achieving low training error but poor validation or test performance. Causes include too little data, excessive complexity, and label noise. Fixes include more data, regularization, simpler models, early stopping, and ensembling.
296: Detect overfitting by comparing training versus validation curves: a growing gap with falling validation performance is the signature. Cross-validation score variance and performance degradation on fresh data confirm it. Learning curves are the primary diagnostic tool.
297: Fix overfitting with more or augmented data, regularization (L1/L2, dropout), early stopping, simpler models or fewer features, ensembles like bagging, and checking for leakage. The best single lever is almost always more representative data.
298: Regularization adds a penalty on model complexity to the loss so the model prefers simpler fits that generalize. L2 shrinks weights smoothly, L1 drives some weights to exactly zero, and in deep learning dropout and weight decay serve the same purpose. The regularization strength is tuned on validation data.
299: L2 (ridge) adds the sum of squared weights to the loss, shrinking weights smoothly and handling correlated features well. L1 (lasso) adds the sum of absolute weights, pushing some coefficients exactly to zero, which performs feature selection. Use L1 for sparsity and interpretability, L2 as the default smoother.
300: Early stopping halts training when validation loss stops improving, keeping the best checkpoint. It prevents the model from drifting into overfitted territory and is nearly free computationally. It is one of the most effective regularizers in deep learning.
301: Data leakage is when information unavailable at prediction time sneaks into training, making offline metrics look great while production fails. Types include target leakage from post-outcome features and train-test contamination via preprocessing fitted on all data. It is the most common cause of the '99% offline, 60% production' disaster.
302: Target leakage occurs when a feature contains information about the outcome that would not exist at prediction time, like 'cancellation_fee' present only for customers who already churned. Such features produce inflated accuracy but are impossible to use live. Audit each feature for when it becomes known.
303: Train-test contamination happens when test data influences training, directly through duplicates shared across splits, or indirectly through preprocessing like scaling and imputation fitted on the whole dataset before splitting. Always split first, then fit preprocessing on train only.
304: Fitting preprocessing on the full dataset lets test-set statistics, like means, scales, and vocabulary, influence training, which is subtle leakage. The train set becomes unrepresentative of truly unseen data, inflating scores. Use pipelines that fit on train and transform validation, test, and production identically.
305: Cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate of generalization than a single split by averaging performance over multiple train-validation partitions. It reduces the luck of one particular split, uses all data for both training and evaluation, and is essential for small datasets and hyperparameter tuning.
306: K-fold cross-validation splits data into K folds, trains on K-1, validates on the held-out fold, and rotates until each fold has been validated once, then averages the scores. It provides a lower-variance estimate of generalization. Typical K is 5 or 10.
307: Stratified K-fold keeps the class proportions in every fold equal to the full dataset. It matters for imbalanced classification, where a random fold might contain almost no minority examples, making validation scores noisy or meaningless. Use it for classification by default.
308: Group K-fold ensures that all rows sharing a group identifier, like the same user, patient, or device, stay in the same fold. It prevents the model from memorizing group-specific patterns and being tested on data from groups it already saw. Essential whenever entities repeat across rows.
309: Time-series cross-validation trains on the past and validates on the future, expanding the window forward, because random splits would let the model see the future. It respects temporal order and tests true forecasting ability. Never shuffle time-ordered data.
310: A lucky split is a train-test partition that happens to favor the model, producing an optimistic score unrepresentative of true performance. It is common with small datasets or skewed classes. Cross-validation and repeated splits guard against it.
311: An unlucky split is the opposite: a partition that unfairly penalizes the model, such as a validation fold with almost no minority class. The fix is the same: stratification, grouping, repeated CV, and judging models on averaged scores rather than one split.
312: Repeatedly tuning against the same test set leaks it into your selection process: you gradually overfit the test set by choosing whatever scores best on it. The reported score then overstates real performance. Keep a final untouched holdout, or use nested cross-validation for tuning.
541: Neural networks earn their complexity when data has non-linear patterns, high dimensions, or interactions that manual feature engineering cannot capture, like images, audio, text, and tabular data with intricate interactions. Universal approximation plus representation learning lets them discover features automatically. For small simple tabular problems, gradient boosting is often still the better choice.
542: A perceptron is the earliest neural unit: it computes a weighted sum of inputs plus bias and outputs a step function. It can only separate classes with a hyperplane, famously failing on XOR. Stacking layers and using differentiable activations fixes this limitation.
543: A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias, and applies a non-linear activation. It is the atomic unit of a neural network. Layers of neurons compose simple functions into complex ones.
544: An activation function introduces non-linearity between layers; without it, any stack of layers collapses into one linear transformation. Common choices are ReLU and its variants for hidden layers, sigmoid for binary output probability, and softmax for multi-class outputs.
545: Sigmoid maps any real number to (0,1) as 1/(1+e^-x), making it a natural probability output for binary classification. Its drawbacks are saturated gradients at both ends, which slow learning, and non-zero-centered outputs. It is mostly used at output layers now, not in hidden layers.
546: Tanh maps values to (-1,1) and is zero-centered, so it generally trains faster than sigmoid. It still saturates for large inputs, killing gradients. It appears in older architectures, RNNs, and as a smooth squashing function.
547: Softmax converts a vector of scores into a probability distribution: exponentiate each score and divide by the sum, so outputs are positive and total 1. It is the standard multi-class output layer, paired with cross-entropy loss. Temperature scales how peaked or flat the resulting distribution is.
548: ReLU (max(0, x)) is the default hidden-layer activation because it is extremely cheap, does not saturate for positive inputs, and gives sparse activations. These properties make gradients flow well and training deep networks practical.
549: ReLU helps because its constant gradient of 1 for positive inputs avoids the vanishing gradients that saturate sigmoid and tanh, its cheap max operation speeds up large networks, and it produces sparse representations. Empirically it unlocked training much deeper networks.
550: Dying ReLU is when a neuron's pre-activation stays negative for all inputs, so its output and gradient are always zero and it never recovers. Causes include too-high learning rates and unlucky initialization. Fixes are lower learning rates, careful init, or leaky ReLU, PReLU, or ELU variants.
551: Forward propagation passes inputs layer by layer, each computing weighted sums plus biases and activations, until the output and loss are produced. It is the model's prediction pass. Its intermediate values are stored for use in backpropagation.
552: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule layer by layer from output back to input, reusing intermediate results efficiently. Those gradients feed the optimizer to update weights. It is the training engine of all modern neural networks.
553: The chain rule lets you differentiate composed functions: the derivative of f(g(x)) is f'(g(x)) times g'(x). Backpropagation is a systematic, matrix-based application of the chain rule across network layers, caching activations to avoid recomputation.
554: Gradient descent iteratively updates parameters in the direction that decreases the loss: theta = theta - lr * gradient. The learning rate controls step size: too large diverges, too small crawls. Variants use different batch sizes for computing each gradient.
555: Batch gradient descent computes the gradient over the entire dataset for each update, giving a stable, exact descent direction but at high cost per step and no inherent stochasticity. It is impractical for large datasets or deep networks.
556: SGD updates weights using the gradient from one sample at a time, making steps fast but noisy; the noise can help escape saddle points. In practice 'SGD' usually means mini-batch SGD, and momentum or Adam variants are used to smooth and accelerate it.
557: Mini-batch gradient descent computes gradients on small batches, typically 32 to 1024 samples, balancing stable gradients with frequent updates and GPU efficiency. It is the standard training method for deep learning, with batch size affecting both speed and generalization.
558: The learning rate is the optimizer's step size. Too high causes divergence or oscillation; too low causes painfully slow training or getting stuck. Schedules like warmup, cosine decay, and step decay adjust it during training and often improve final results significantly.
559: An iteration is one parameter update using one batch; a batch is the subset of samples per update; an epoch is one full pass over the training data. With 1,000 samples and batch size 100, one epoch has 10 iterations. These terms define training schedules and logging.
560: Weight initialization sets starting values before training. Poor init, all zeros or badly scaled, causes symmetric neurons or exploding/vanishing activations. Modern schemes keep activation variance stable across layers, which is crucial for deep networks to train at all.
561: Xavier (Glorot) initialization draws weights with variance scaled to 1/fan_in (or 2/(fan_in+fan_out)), designed for sigmoid and tanh activations to keep signal variance stable through layers. It is the standard choice for tanh-based networks.
562: He initialization scales variance by 2/fan_in, compensating for ReLU zeroing out negative half of its inputs. It is the default for ReLU networks and helps deep layers avoid vanishing activations.
563: Vanishing gradients occur when gradients shrink exponentially while flowing backward through saturating activations or deep layers, so early layers barely learn. Causes include sigmoid/tanh saturation and deep unnormalized stacks. Fixes: ReLU-family activations, batch/layer normalization, residual connections, and careful initialization.
564: Exploding gradients occur when gradients grow exponentially backward, causing wild parameter updates and divergent loss. Common in RNNs and unnormalized deep nets. Fixes include gradient clipping, normalization layers, residual connections, and lower learning rates.
565: Gradient clipping caps gradient norm at a threshold, rescaling when it exceeds it, so a single pathological batch cannot blow up the weights. It is essential for RNNs and LLM training where loss spikes happen. It trades a slightly noisy step for training stability.
566: Batch normalization normalizes layer inputs across the batch dimension using running statistics at inference, reducing internal covariate shift. It stabilizes and speeds training, allows higher learning rates, and has a mild regularizing effect from batch noise. It struggles with tiny batches and sequential models.
567: Layer normalization normalizes across each sample's features rather than across the batch, so it works identically in training and inference and is batch-size independent. It is the standard in Transformers and RNNs where batch statistics are awkward or unavailable.
568: Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training, forcing redundant, distributed representations and preventing co-adaptation. At inference it is disabled, with scales calibrated during training. It is a cheap, effective regularizer for fully connected and attention layers.
569: Weight decay adds an L2 penalty on weights to the loss (or equivalently shrinks weights each update in AdamW), discouraging large weights and smoothing the learned function. It reduces overfitting and interacts with learning rate in AdamW, where decoupling it from the adaptive update gives better results.
570: Early stopping monitors validation loss and stops training when it stops improving for a patience window, restoring the best weights. It prevents overfitting late in training and acts as a free regularizer combined with learning-rate schedules.
571: Training loss is measured on the data the model is learning from; validation loss is measured on held-out data. Their gap is the primary signal of generalization health. Both falling is healthy; diverging gap means overfitting; both high means underfitting.
572: Training loss falls while validation loss rises when the model starts memorizing training-specific noise instead of learning general patterns, the textbook signature of overfitting. Remedies: more data or augmentation, regularization, early stopping at the validation minimum, or a smaller model.
573: Overfitting in deep learning is caused by excess capacity relative to data (too many parameters), insufficient or unrepresentative data, training too long without early stopping, missing regularization (dropout, weight decay, augmentation), label noise memorization, and sometimes leakage inflating training performance.
574: Debug a non-learning network by first overfitting a tiny subset: if it cannot hit near-zero loss on 10 samples, something is broken. Then check the loss function matches the task, labels and inputs are aligned and correctly encoded, the learning rate is sane, gradients flow (inspect norms), initialization and normalization are right, and data preprocessing matches the deployment pipeline.
651: Transformers were introduced to fix RNNs' sequential bottleneck: they process all tokens in parallel, scale on GPUs, and capture long-range dependencies directly via self-attention instead of passing information step by step. This unlocked training on massive datasets, which is the foundation of modern LLMs.
652: Self-attention lets every token directly gather information from every other token in one step, so path length between distant tokens is O(1) rather than growing with sequence length like RNNs. It also parallelizes across tokens, unlike recurrence. The cost is quadratic attention computation in sequence length.
653: Attention is a learned mechanism that computes a weighted combination of value vectors, where the weights come from the similarity between a token's query and other tokens' keys. It dynamically routes relevant context to each position. It is differentiable, so the model learns what to attend to.
654: Query is what a token is looking for, Key is what each token offers for matching, and Value is the content each token contributes if attended to. Similarity between Q and K determines attention weights, which then mix V vectors. Separating them allows asymmetric, learned information routing.
655: Three separate projections give the model flexibility to decouple 'what I search for' from 'what I advertise' and 'what I deliver'. If Q=K=V were the same vector, attention weights would be forced to be symmetric similarity and the mixing would be far less expressive. Separate learned spaces make attention powerful.
656: Scaled dot-product attention computes QK^T to score all query-key pairs, scales by sqrt(d_k), optionally masks, softmaxes the scores into weights, and multiplies by V. The formula is softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V. It is the core operation of every Transformer layer.
657: Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the dot products' variance stable as key dimension grows: without it, dot products scale with d_k, pushing softmax into saturated regions with vanishing gradients. The scaling keeps gradients healthy regardless of head dimension.
658: Self-attention attends within the same sequence: each token attends to the others in its own sentence. Cross-attention attends from one sequence to another, like decoder tokens querying encoder outputs in translation, or text queries attending to image patches in multimodal models.
659: Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel in smaller subspaces, concatenates their outputs, and projects once. Each head can specialize, one for syntax, another for coreference, and so on. It increases expressiveness at similar computational cost.
660: Multiple heads let the model attend to different relationships simultaneously: one head might track the subject of a sentence, another nearby positions, another long-range references. A single averaged attention pattern would force a compromise among these needs.
661: Positional encoding injects token order information because self-attention is permutation-invariant: shuffled inputs give shuffled, otherwise identical outputs. Positions are added to embeddings via fixed sinusoids or learned vectors so the model can distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'.
662: Sinusoidal positional encoding uses sine and cosine waves of geometrically increasing frequencies added to token embeddings. It generalizes to lengths unseen in training and requires no learned parameters. Relative offsets have linear relations that attention can exploit.
663: Learned positional embeddings are trainable vectors assigned to each position index, like BERT's. They can encode dataset-specific position patterns and often perform slightly better within the trained range, but they cap the maximum context length and do not extrapolate beyond it.
664: RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) encodes position by rotating query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their positions, so the attention score between two tokens depends only on their relative offset. It is the dominant scheme in modern LLMs like Llama.
665: RoPE solves extrapolation and relativity: attention becomes a function of relative positions, which transfers better to longer sequences than absolute learned embeddings, and it can be extended with techniques like linear interpolation or NTK-aware scaling to stretch context windows cheaply.
666: The encoder maps an input sequence to contextual representations using bidirectional self-attention, seeing the whole input, which suits understanding tasks. The decoder generates outputs left to right using causal self-attention plus cross-attention to the encoder. Encoder-only models like BERT excel at classification; decoder-only models like GPT at generation.
